issues.description: Predicate reads awkwardly; extract a named helper like `isLayerStatement(node)`.
issues.detail: `!(nodeName === 'layer' && typeof node.nodes === 'undefined')` buries the rule in a double negation. The data distinction is layer-statement (allowed) vs. layer-with-block (not). A named helper or positive phrasing at the call site makes intent obvious to the next maintainer.

issues.description: Replace `typeof node.nodes === 'undefined'` with `node.nodes == null` to match PostCSS/codebase idiom.
issues.detail: PostCSS represents block-less at-rules with `nodes` absent and block-having ones with an array. `node.nodes == null` is shorter, conventional in this codebase, and matches the data shape directly. The `typeof` form is defensive verbiage for a value PostCSS controls.

issues.description: Add an accept-case test for statement-form `@layer foo;` before `@import`.
issues.detail: The new test covers the bug (layer-with-block rejected), but no test pins the complementary case: a block-less `@layer foo;` before `@import` must still be accepted. Without it, a future refactor of the predicate could silently regress the allowed behavior. One extra fixture closes the loop.

synthesis.summary: Small, scoped, correct patch that distinguishes `@layer foo;` (statement, allowed before `@import`) from `@layer foo {}` (block, not allowed). All three reviewers converge on the same three nits, none blocking: the inline negated predicate would read better as a named helper, `typeof === 'undefined'` should be `== null` to match codebase idiom, and the test suite needs a paired accept-case for the statement form to lock the invariant from both sides. Verdict: accept after trivial cleanup.
